extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th-century travel literature / historians of the Sahara
extracted.subtask_description: A first-person 19th-century travelogue chapter describing customs, social norms, caravan practices, slavery trade, and everyday life in Ghat (Sahara). Intended for general readers interested in exploration and ethnographic observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caravan conduct customary privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an established custom or law, in The Desert, that the people of each district or country shall enjoy the privilege of conducting the caravans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: the Touaricks of Ghat conduct merchants from Ghadames to Ghat, the Touaricks of Aheer conduct merchants from Ghat to Aheer, and so on along the route to Kanou. This is treated as a norm organizing caravan leadership and local economic rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift-giving to chiefs and travellers' present etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Travellers are expected to give presents en route to various chiefs and local leaders; presenting gifts secures friendship and protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes giving a 'shumlah' (sash) to the Governor and small medical or personal items to chiefs and women; footnote: 'Sunbul' (stalks) is brought into The Desert and 'No present is made to a man of family without sunbul.' A sample budget itemises 'Presents, en route' (13 dollars) as a major travel expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touarick salutation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Touarghee (Touarick) salute: deliberately elevate the right hand to face level, turn the outspread palm to the individual, and slowly say 'Sălām Aleikoum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as simple, elegant and colder than English salutation; when used differently (with menacing raised palm) similar gestures among Moors and Arabs function as curses. Door-posts and rooms are imprinted with the outspread hand to ward off the 'eye-malign.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Local punishment and satisfaction for violent acts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a violent act occurs (example: assault on a man at prayer), local authority gives satisfaction to the injured party, which may include confiscation of the offender's property and expulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Touarghee wounded a Ghadamsee during prayer; the Marabout Governor 'stripped the house of the Touraghee of all his little property, turned him out into the street, and ordered him immediately to leave Ghat.' This indicates customary remedies for personal violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marabout/governor role and gift-taking norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious leaders (marabouts) may disclaim temporal authority but in practice decide affairs and accept presents like secular sheikhs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Haj Ahmed repeatedly said 'I am not Sheikh... I'm only Marabout,' yet he received presents, acted as governor, owned land and slaves, and ruled on local matters. Travelers were expected to present gifts to secure favor from such figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desert slave-trade practices and economics
rubrics_metrics.description: Slave markets in Saharan towns involve purchase and resale across routes; prices, duties, credit from European merchants, and poor provisioning en route are central features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: slaves bought at forty mahboubs and sold at sixty in Tripoli with a ten-duty to the Pasha; traders like Haj Ibrahim obtain goods on credit from European merchants and exchange them for slaves to pay bills; many slaves are fed only on dates en route and many die before arrival. The narrative treats these as normal economic mechanisms of the slave-traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local medical practice preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Saharan people generally prefer their own remedies and poultices over European medicine, even when asking European advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: injured man poulticed his hand with wet clay and camel's dung despite the author's suggestion of a bread poultice; slaves were often given meagre food rather than medicine. The author notes people may 'condescend to ask you your advice' but keep to traditional remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical budgeting for Saharan caravans
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelers should budget specifically for presents, staple foods, and minor extras rather than luxuries; example budget for route Ghat to Kanou totaled about 22 dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample budget items listed: Presents en route to various chiefs (13 dollars), Wheat and bread (5), Olive-oil and 'semen' (liquid butter) (1), Extras/unforeseen expenses (3). The author emphasizes that nothing was listed for meat or tea/sugar — common luxuries rarely consumed by Saharan merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious religious conduct for foreign travelers
rubrics_metrics.description: A European traveler should avoid openly offending or denouncing Islam and must practice tact in religious discussion to avoid endangering himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains frequent evasions on religious questions and explicitly states he refused to adopt Muslim practices even under pressure; warns that any disrespect for Muhammad 'would have exposed me to be torn to pieces by the rabble.' He defends maintaining Christian confession as a matter of conscience and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local hospitality and small gifts as social currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Small acts of hospitality (offering tea, biscuits, dates) quickly secure friendship and social access in Ghat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: giving two cups of tea, a little sugar and two biscuits 'made him my friend for ever; a cheap purchase of eternal friendship.' The narrative emphasizes how modest gifts create social bonds and entry to households.
